blocks.text: BC rules for park tenancies and 55+ parks
If you buy a home in a park, you buy the home and take over a pad tenancy. These are the rules that decide what you can and cannot do.

v.t: A person who owns a manufactured home and rents the site it sits on.
A home on land the owner also owns goes through the land title system instead.
If you rent the home and the site from an owner, the Residential Tenancy Act applies, not this Act.
In a designated 55-plus park, at least one tenant on the site must be 55 or older.
A park can state its rule more strictly. One Aldergrove co-op listing requires both occupants to be 55.
The park’s tenancy agreement and rules apply, not strata age bylaws, which cover strata corporations only.
When a home sells, the existing pad tenancy is assigned to the buyer.
The seller must give you any written part of the tenancy agreement and the written park rules before asking the park owner to consent.
Made in writing on RTB Form 10 and needs the park owner’s consent.
The owner’s response must reach the home owner by the 10th day. No response by then means consent is deemed given.
The park owner cannot charge a fee or take a benefit for consenting.
You become the tenant on the same terms as before.
Once every 12 months, with at least 3 full months’ notice.
The 12-month average change in the BC Consumer Price Index, plus a share of the change in local government levies and regulated park utilities, divided by the number of sites in the park.
The Manufactured Home Park Tenancy Regulation.
Park rules are part of the tenancy agreement.
They apply to all tenants fairly, are clear, are properly noticed and do not change a material term.
Since the April 30, 2024 regulation change, rules can change once a year with three months’ notice.
The owner must have all government permits and approvals in place.
12 months’ notice to end the tenancy.
$20,000 to the tenant on or before the notice takes effect.
You can leave on 10 days’ written notice and pay rent to the move-out date.
A sale is only effective if it is registered in the province’s Manufactured Home Registry, run through BC Registries.
The signed Bill of Sale and Notice to Transfer or Change Ownership are filed by a lawyer or notary.
The CSA certification label must be on the home at the sale.

There is no province-wide park zoning. Each city zones parks in its own bylaw.

Some cities add a policy. Surrey’s Manufactured Home Park Policy walks residents through the 12-month notice, permits-first and $20,000 compensation steps, and names help groups including the BC Manufactured Home Owners association and the Tenant Resource & Advisory Centre.

blocks.text: How to Buy a Mobile Home in BC: how mobile and manufactured homes work here

items.t: A home on a rented pad is not land ownership: In a pad-rental park the buyer owns the home — a chattel, registered in the Manufactured Home Registry — and rents the pad from the park owner under a Manufactured Home Site Tenancy Agreement. There is no land title, no strata lot and no Form B in this form.

Own-land manufactured-home stock is a different stock: In a bare-land strata park the buyer owns the lot as a strata lot — Form B, strata fees and registered bylaws apply, and there is no pad rent. In a co-operative the land is held through the co-op and the buyer holds a co-op interest plus the home. On fee-simple land the buyer owns the parcel outright.

The two ownership forms the guide is built around: (1) you own the home and rent the pad (site) it sits on in a manufactured home park — the land is the park owner's; (2) you own both the home and the land it sits on.

Zoning for parks is municipal, not provincial: there is no province-wide park zoning — each municipality zones manufactured home parks in its own bylaw; for example, Surrey's Zoning Bylaw No. 12000 has a Manufactured Home Residential Zone (RM-M) permitting manufactured home parks, and Maple Ridge's Zoning Bylaw 7600-2019 has an RMH Manufactured Home Park Residential zone.

blocks.text: Local rules that affect park-home buyers

items.t: Pad rent increases: A landlord may increase pad rent once every 12 months, with at least 3 full months' written notice, capped by formula — the inflation rate (the 12-month average change in the BC all-items Consumer Price Index) plus a proportional amount (the change in local government levies plus the change in regulated park utilities, divided by the number of manufactured home sites in the park); the landlord may not round up and may not carry forward an unused portion of a prior year's limit. The caps verified live from the RTB (Nov 1, 2026): 2026 = 2.3% + proportional amount; 2027 = 2.2% + proportional amount.

Age rules in parks are park designations, not strata bylaws: The Province states the general rule for a designated 55-plus park: at least one tenant on the site must be 55 years of age or older. Individual parks can state their occupancy rule more strictly in their own documents, so the park's own tenancy agreement and rules are the operative document.

Municipal layer on top of the Act: Some cities add a park-redevelopment policy on top of the MHPTA; Surrey's Manufactured Home Park Policy brochure, for example, walks residents through the 12-month notice, permits-first and $20,000 compensation steps and names help organizations including the BC Manufactured Home Owners association and the Tenant Resource & Advisory Centre.

June 6, 2018: The Province's information bulletin states the new compensation for tenants of manufactured home parks facing eviction took effect June 6, 2018: compensation on a park closure/conversion became a flat $20,000, increased from the previous requirement of 12 months of pad rental costs; the same changes require park owners to compensate tenants for the assessed value of the home over $20,000 where the manufactured home cannot be relocated, clarify that a tenant unable to relocate the home is not responsible for disposal costs, and set bad-faith closure compensation at 12 months' pad rental or $5,000, whichever is greater.

2019: The Province's September 4, 2019 release states rent increase limits are tied only to the inflation rate (the 12-month average percentage change in the BC Consumer Price Index), and that for manufactured home park tenancies the rate is that inflation figure plus a proportional amount for changes in local government levies and regulated utility fees — the formula structure still in use, whose verified outputs are 2.3% + proportional (2026) and 2.2% + proportional (2027).

April 30, 2024: The Province announced April 30, 2024 that changes to the Manufactured Home Park Tenancy Regulation mean park owners may change park rules only once per year, must give tenants three months' notice of a rule change (up from two weeks), and must give that notice on a form approved by the Residential Tenancy Branch.

October 20, 2025: Surrey adopted its Tenant Protection Bylaw No. 21788 and Rental Replacement Policy No. O-63 on October 20, 2025 for multi-unit rental redevelopment, and the bylaw does not apply to property governed by the Manufactured Home Park Tenancy Act — a dated reminder that park residents' redevelopment protection remains the provincial 12-month notice and $20,000 framework plus any city park policy, not the new city bylaw.

blocks.text: The rules for buying in a park
Pad tenancy, park-owner consent, pad-rent caps and the Manufactured Home Registry are explained on their own page.

faq.a: No — in a pad-rental park you own the home and rent the site under a pad tenancy agreement; the Manufactured Home Park Tenancy Act applies to a person who owns a manufactured home and rents the site it sits on. The exceptions in prove the rule: in a bare-land strata park such as Sea Ridge Bays you own the lot as a strata lot, and in a co-operative such as Pioneer Park the land is held through the co-op.
faq.q: If I buy a mobile home in a park, do I own the land?

faq.a: The home is registered in the Manufactured Home Registry rather than dealt with as land title real property, and the transfer is only effective once registered, filed through a lawyer or notary with the signed Bill of Sale and Notice to Transfer or Change Ownership.
faq.q: How is financing different for a home on a rented pad?

faq.a: The sale needs the park owner's prior written consent to assign the tenancy — but the owner must respond within 10 days of the written request (RTB Form 10), silence counts as consent given, and no fee can be charged for consent. Listings phrase this as "subject to park approval".
faq.q: Can the park owner refuse to let me buy a home in the park?

faq.a: Once every 12 months, on at least 3 full months' notice, by no more than the inflation rate (BC consumer price index) plus a proportional amount for the park's changes in local government levies and regulated utilities, divided by the number of sites in the park. For scale, the RTB's own rent-increase form for manufactured home sites states the formula outcome as 3% plus the proportional amount for increases effective in 2025, and 2.3% plus the proportional amount for increases effective in 2026.
faq.q: How much can my pad rent go up each year?

faq.a: The Act's framework assumes a home can be relocated — the closure-compensation rules even add compensation where a home cannot be moved. What is fixed in law is the paperwork: any later sale or transfer is only effective once registered in the Manufactured Home Registry, and the CSA certification label must be attached to the home at the point of sale — a missing label is a red flag for moving, financing and resale.
faq.q: Can I move my home to another park later?

faq.a: A sale of the park alone does not end your tenancy — your assigned tenancy continues on the same terms. A conversion of all or a significant part of the park is different: the landlord must have all permits and approvals first, give 12 months' notice, and pay you $20,000 compensation on or before the notice's effective date; you may leave early on at least 10 days' written notice.
faq.q: What happens if the park is sold or redeveloped?

faq.a: Yes, as a park designation under the provincial framework: the Province states that in a designated 55-plus park at least one tenant on the site must be 55 years of age or older. This is a different legal mechanism from a strata's 55+ bylaw — do not apply strata exemption rules to a pad tenancy; read the park's tenancy agreement and rules, which can state the occupancy rule more strictly.
faq.q: Is a park's 55+ age restriction legally valid?

faq.a: The written tenancy agreement and the written park rules — the regulation requires the seller to give the proposed purchaser both before the park owner is even asked to consent to the assignment — plus the current pad rent and the date of the last increase, so the increase formula can be checked.
faq.q: What paperwork should the seller hand me before I write an offer?

faq.a: Yes — a manufactured home owner is assessed and taxed like other residential property owners, but the assessed value does not include the value of the land when the home is in a manufactured home park not on reserve land. Some parks include the land portion of property taxes inside the pad rent (Westwood Estates and Val Maria listings both state this) — check what the specific park's pad rent includes.
faq.q: Do I pay property tax on a home I own on a rented pad?

faq.a: Ask the park for its current tenancy agreement and park rules in writing before relying on either claim.
faq.q: A directory calls a park 55+, but a listing in it says no age restrictions. Which is right?

faq.a: Get the current pad rent from the park's written Manufactured Home Site Tenancy Agreement for the specific home, never from a web range.
